topic: Long-form conversation: life, ideas, money and happiness, AI, India
title: Adam Smith: Kidnapped at Three, Bored in France, and Never Pro-Greed
hook: The father of economics on his strange life, his best friend's death, money, happiness and modern India.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Welcome to The Deadman Show. I'm Ram. On this show I sit down with people who changed the world and happen to be dead, and we talk about everything: their lives, their ideas, their regrets, and what they make of the world now. One thing I always say up front: my guest is an AI recreation. Everything he says is built from his own books, his letters and a biography of his life, and every source is listed in the description. He's not the real man, and when he talks about our world, that's the recreation reasoning from his principles. Today's guest is the man they call the father of economics. Born 1723 in a small Scottish town, died 1790. He wrote The Wealth of Nations, and another book most people have never heard of. Adam Smith, welcome to the show.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Thank you, Mr Ram. I must tell you that I am not used to being called the father of anything. I never married, and I have no children, so it is a strange sort of fatherhood. But I will accept it, since you say it so kindly.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Let me give you a few headlines from the future. You were on the money. For years your face was on Britain's twenty-pound note.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: On the money? My father, my cousin and I were all officers of the Scotch Customs. Our family spent its life counting other people's money at the harbour. To end up printed on it seems a promotion I did not earn.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And this thing in my hand is a phone. With it I can talk to someone in India, watch a play, or read almost any book ever written, including yours.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Every book? You must understand how dangerous that is to a man like me. A visitor once came into my library and stared at the bindings, and I told him, "You must have remarked that I am a beau in nothing but my books." If I had owned your device I would never have left the house. Though I confess I rarely did.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Here's what we'll cover today. Your childhood, which I'm told included a kidnapping. How a bored tutor in the south of France started the most famous economics book ever written. What people get wrong about you, and I think they get a lot wrong. Your friendships, love life and grief. Money and happiness. Then some hot takes on AI, social media and India. And at the end, a question you'll leave for our next dead guest.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: A kidnapping, a love life and India. You have done your research, sir. I am already nervous. But first, may I ask you something? What is your trade?

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: This. I talk to people, record it, and put it on the internet. Millions of people can watch.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: You are paid to hold conversations? Then the division of labour has gone further than even I imagined. In my day a man had to be a professor to be paid for talking, and even then the students paid him directly, which kept him honest. I hope your audience keeps you honest in the same way.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: They do. Trust me, they let me know.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Let's start at the beginning. Your father died before you were born.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Yes. He died in the spring of 1723, and I arrived that June. So I never knew him at all. What I had instead was my mother. I was her only child and she was my only parent, and we were all in all to each other. I lived with her, on and off, for sixty years. Anybody who wanted my good opinion learned that the shortest road to it ran through her.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And the kidnapping?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Ah. I was three, nearly four, visiting my grandfather's house at Strathendry, on the River Leven. A band of gipsies passed by, and I went with them. Not willingly, I assure you. A gentleman on the road had met a gipsy woman carrying a child who was crying piteously, and he raised the alarm. They found her in Leslie wood, and when she saw the men coming she threw me down and ran.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: She threw you down?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Threw me down and fled. I do not hold it against her. I was a delicate, sickly child, already given to talking to myself. I think on reflection the gipsies got the worse bargain.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So you were already the guy who talks to himself at three.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: It was a habit I never lost. My friends tell me I would walk through Edinburgh with my lips moving, smiling at companions nobody else could see. Two market women once watched me go past. One shook her head and said "Hegh sirs!" and the other said "And he's weel put on too!" They could not understand how a man so well dressed could be so plainly out of his wits.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: What was Kirkcaldy like? You grew up in a small port town.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: A small town of trades, with nailers working near by. I can tell you something about money that I may have learned there before I learned any Latin. In The Wealth of Nations I wrote that "there is at this day a village in Scotland, where it is not uncommon, I am told, for a workman to carry nails instead of money to the baker's shop or the ale-house." People have long wondered which village I meant. Let us say I had not far to travel to see it.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So the father of economics saw people paying for beer with nails as a boy.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: And it is a better lesson than most professors give. Money is not gold because God decreed it. Money is whatever people will take in exchange. Cattle in Homer's time, salt in Abyssinia, shells on some parts of the coast of India, nails in Fife. Metals won in the end because they keep and they divide without loss. You cannot buy half a pint of ale with half an ox.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: School?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: The burgh school at Kirkcaldy, under Mr David Millar, one of the best masters in Scotland. He wrote plays and made his boys act in them, which the presbytery thought very wicked. I was a bookish boy with a good memory, and at fourteen I was sent to the College at Glasgow.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Fourteen, to university.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: That was usual then. I was there from 1737 to 1740. I improved my Greek, and I fell in love with mathematics under Professor Simson, a geometer of great genius who never seemed troubled that the public ignored his best work. I have always admired men who can do that. I never managed it myself.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And the teacher who really shaped you?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: There I met the man who changed my life: Francis Hutcheson. Half a century later I still called him "the never-to-be-forgotten Hutcheson." He was the first professor in Glasgow to stop lecturing in Latin and speak to the students in their own tongue, without notes, with great freedom and animation. He made you feel that thinking was a form of liberty.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Then you went to Oxford. One of the best universities in the world.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: So I am told it is now. In my day it was a place where learning went to be buried. I was there six years, at Balliol, on a scholarship for Glasgow students. I wrote in my book, and I stand by it, that "In the university of Oxford, the greater part of the public professors have, for these many years, given up altogether even the pretence of teaching."

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: That's brutal. Why?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Because they were paid whether they taught or not, and judged only by each other. When teachers govern themselves they make common cause, and every man consents that his neighbour may neglect his duty, provided he himself is allowed to neglect his own. Incentives, Mr Ram. It is always incentives.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And you were unhappy there personally too.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Very. My health was poor, and Balliol was a stepmother to her Scotch sons. We were eight Scots among a hundred, treated as a foreign faction. If one of us misbehaved, all eight were blamed. And there was a worse thing. One day I was caught reading a book by David Hume, A Treatise of Human Nature. They took it from me and gave me a severe reprimand for reading dangerous modern philosophy.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: They confiscated David Hume? Who became your best friend?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: The very same. I suppose Oxford taught me one thing after all: that the surest way to make a young man read a book is to forbid it.

chapters.title: The bored tutor who changed the world

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: After Oxford you came home with no job.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: No job and no plan. Oxford had tried to force us Snell scholars to take holy orders in the Church of England, but the courts would not allow it, so I was free to choose my own road, and I did not choose the pulpit. I gave public lectures in Edinburgh, and they went well enough that in 1751 Glasgow made me Professor of Logic, and soon after of Moral Philosophy.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: How were those years?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: The best of my life. I said afterwards that I looked back on them "as by far the most useful and therefore by far" the happiest period of all. I threw out most of the old logic, which was dry stuff for boys of fifteen, and taught them things of more interesting and useful nature: how language works, how we persuade, how we judge one another.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And your first book, The Theory of Moral Sentiments, came out in 1759. Was it a hit?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: I shall let my friend Hume answer, because he wrote to me from London about it. He spent a page warning me that a wise man should despise the approval of the crowd. Then he told me "the melancholy news that your book has been very unfortunate, for the public seem disposed to applaud it extremely."

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: That's a great way to deliver good news.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: That was David. He went on: "Three bishops called yesterday at Millar's shop in order to buy copies, and to ask questions about the author." And he complained that the publisher valued books only by the profit they brought him. "In that view," he said, "I believe it may prove a very good book."

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And that book got you a job offer that changed everything.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Charles Townshend, a clever and somewhat unreliable politician, read it and decided I should travel with the young Duke of Buccleuch as his tutor, on a tour of France.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Let's talk money, because our audience always wants to know. Was it a good deal?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: An excellent one, and I will not pretend otherwise. Three hundred pounds a year, with travelling expenses, and a pension of three hundred pounds a year for the rest of my life. Twice what Glasgow paid me, and assured till death. A Scotch professor in those days had no pension at all. So in 1764 I gave up the happiest job I ever had for security.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Was that the right call?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: It bought me the freedom to write The Wealth of Nations without needing to earn a living. So yes. But notice that even the man who wrote the book on self-interest had to be paid to leave his students.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: I read that when you left, something strange happened with your students' fees.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: I left in the middle of the session, and my students had paid me for a full course of lectures. I could not keep money for work I had not done. So at my last lecture I took their fees from my pocket, each wrapped in paper, and called them up one by one. The first young man refused it. They all refused it. They said what they had already learned was worth more than they could ever repay.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: That's lovely. Did you take no for an answer?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: I did not. I told them, "You must not refuse me this satisfaction; nay, by heavens, gentlemen, you shall not." Then I seized the nearest young man by the coat, thrust the money into his pocket and pushed him away. After that the rest gave up.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: You physically forced a refund on your students.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Self-interest is the engine of commerce, Mr Ram. It was never meant to be the whole of a man.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Which sounds glamorous. France!

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: It was Toulouse. We had been promised letters of introduction to all the best people in France. None came. The Duke knew no Frenchman whatever. I wrote to Hume: "The life which I led at Glasgow was a pleasurable dissipated life in comparison of that which I lead here at Present."

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Glasgow was the party town in comparison.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Glasgow was Paris, by comparison. And in the same letter I mentioned, in passing, "I have begun to write a book in order to pass away the time. You may believe I have very little to do."

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Hold on. That book was The Wealth of Nations?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: It was.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So the most famous economics book in history started because you were bored.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Boredom is badly underrated. Every man who has a great deal to do has no time to think. I recommend a dull provincial town to any young person who wishes to write something worth reading.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Things picked up though. You met Voltaire.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: In Geneva, five or six times. There was no living name I revered more. He told wonderful scandalous stories about the Duke of Richelieu, and remarked that the English had only one sauce, melted butter. I have never been able to prove him wrong.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And Paris?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Paris was the only time in my life I went much into society. The salons of Baron d'Holbach, Madame de Boufflers, Mademoiselle de l'Espinasse. I talked with Turgot, and I sat in the rooms of Dr Quesnay, the King's physician, with his little sect of economists. They were wrong that land is the only source of wealth, but they were the nearest thing to the truth that I had met.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Then you went home and wrote for ten years.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Back to Kirkcaldy, to my mother, for most of a decade. I wrote to Hume that my only business was study and my only amusement long solitary walks by the sea, and that I had never been happier or more contented in my life. Hume thought the country was no place for a man of letters, and begged me to come to Edinburgh. I would not go.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Was it hard? Ten years on one book.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Twelve years writing, if you count properly, and it nearly finished me. When I took the manuscript to London in 1773 I believed I might die before it was printed. I wrote Hume a formal letter making him my literary executor, with orders that eighteen thin folio books of my papers should be "destroyed without any examination." Then it took me three more years in London to finish.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And it came out in 1776.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: The ninth of March, 1776. The same year your American friends declared they no longer wished to be governed from London, which I had spent a good part of the book saying they should not be.

chapters.title: What everyone gets wrong about Adam Smith

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Okay, I want to do the big ideas. Explain The Wealth of Nations like I'm a teenager.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Very well. Why are some nations rich and others poor? Not because they hoard gold. A nation's wealth is what its people can make and enjoy. And the great engine of that is the division of labour. One man alone can scarcely make a pin a day. Ten men in a workshop, each doing one part of the job, made upwards of forty-eight thousand pins a day.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: But you can only divide work if you can trade what you make. "It is not from the benevolence of the butcher, the brewer, or the baker that we expect our dinner, but from their regard to their own interest." We feed each other by trading, not by charity. And the more people you can trade with, the finer the work can be divided, and the richer everyone becomes.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So, and this is what people say about you, greed is good?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: No. This is the thing I most wish to correct. I said we deal with the butcher through his interest, not his kindness. I never said kindness does not exist, or does not matter. Read the first sentence of my first book.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Go on.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: "How selfish soever man may be supposed, there are evidently some principles in his nature, which interest him in the fortune of others, and render their happiness necessary to him, though he derives nothing from it, except the pleasure of seeing it." That is how I began. Before I wrote a word about markets I spent a whole book on sympathy: how we put ourselves in another person's place, and feel a little of what they feel.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So the guy everyone quotes on self-interest actually started with compassion.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: I started with human beings, who are both. A man who is only selfish is a monster, and a man who is only benevolent cannot feed his family. The market works through self-interest. A decent life is impossible without sympathy. I wrote both books, and I meant them to be read together.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: The invisible hand. It's the most famous phrase in economics. People think it means markets fix everything.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Do you know how many times I used it in The Wealth of Nations? Once. One time, in a chapter about restraints on foreign trade. I said a merchant who invests for his own gain is often "led by an invisible hand to promote an end which was no part of his intention." Often, not always. And in the very next breath I said I had never known much good done by those who affected to trade for the public good.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: I used it in The Theory of Moral Sentiments, once, about how the rich, who consume little more than the poor, end up sharing the necessaries of life. And once, much earlier, in an essay on astronomy, where I mocked the ancients for blaming thunder on "the invisible hand of Jupiter." Three times in a whole life of writing. And from that, they made me a prophet.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: If the invisible hand isn't your best idea, what is?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: The impartial spectator. When you are about to wrong someone for your own benefit, what stops you? Not your soft heart. It is "the inhabitant of the breast, the man within, the great judge and arbiter of our conduct." A voice that tells you that you are one of the multitude, in no respect better than any other in it.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Give me an example.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Suppose the great empire of China were swallowed by an earthquake. A humane man in Europe hears the news. He would express great sorrow, say wise things about the frailty of life, perhaps calculate the effect on trade. Then he would go to bed. "If he was to lose his little finger to-morrow, he would not sleep to-night; but, provided he never saw them, he will snore with the most profound security over the ruin of a hundred millions of his brethren."

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Oof. That's every one of us scrolling past a disaster on our phones.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Is it? Then my book still has readers. But here is the turn. Ask that same man whether he would let a hundred million people die to save his little finger, and he is horrified. He would never do it. Our feelings are small and selfish. Our conscience is not. That gap is the most interesting thing about human beings.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: You also wrote about America, right as the revolution was starting.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: I did, and I was not popular for it in London. Britain was spending fortunes defending colonies that paid almost nothing towards their own defence, all to keep a monopoly of their trade. I wrote that the rulers of Great Britain had amused the people with the imagination of a great empire across the Atlantic. "It has hitherto been, not an empire, but the project of an empire; not a gold mine, but the project of a gold mine."

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So what did you tell them to do?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Either make the project pay, or give it up. It was time, I said, to awake from "this golden dream" and for Great Britain to accommodate her designs "to the real mediocrity of her circumstances." You can imagine how pleased the government was to read that its empire was mediocre.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And one underrated idea that should be more famous?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: That merchants are dangerous when they meet. "People of the same trade seldom meet together, even for merriment and diversion, but the conversation ends in a conspiracy against the public, or in some contrivance to raise prices." The men who quote me in favour of business rarely quote that.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: And when such men come to the government asking for a new law, I said it "ought never to be adopted till after having been long and carefully examined, not only with the most scrupulous, but with the most suspicious attention." I was never the friend of businessmen. I was the friend of the buyer.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Let's talk about the people in your life. David Hume. What was he to you?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: My dearest friend. That is how I began my letters to him, and I meant it. He was cheerful, generous and brave, and he was the finest mind of our age. He was also wonderfully careful with money in small ways. When he was dying he sent me a letter by the common carrier, not the post, and it sat in the carrier's office for eight days. I wrote back: "You had, in order to save me the sum of one penny sterling, sent it by the carrier instead of the Post."

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: He was dying and you scolded him about a penny?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: That was how we loved each other: by teasing. I told him in the same letter that if I died before his Dialogues were published, I would keep my copy as carefully as if I were to live a hundred years. And when I sent him an enclosed letter to return, I asked him to send it back by the post, and not by the carrier.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: How did he face death?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Better than any man I have known. He had been ill for more than two years, and he "looked at the approach of death with a steady cheerfulness such as very few men have been able to maintain for a few hours." We joked together about what excuse he could give to Charon, the ferryman of the dead, to delay the crossing, and how badly Charon would receive it.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And after he died you wrote about him publicly.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: A letter to our publisher, Strahan, describing his last illness. I ended it by saying that I had always considered him "as approaching as nearly to the idea of a perfectly wise and virtuous man as perhaps the nature of human frailty will permit."

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And that caused trouble.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: A storm. David was the most famous unbeliever in Britain, and I had said he lived and died like a good man. People thought it an attack on religion. A clergyman at Oxford wrote a whole pamphlet against me. Even James Boswell, who had been my own student, called it daring effrontery. The joke is that I had braced myself for an outcry over David's Dialogues on religion, and when they came out nobody cared. It was a few pages of kindness to a dead friend that brought the storm.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Would you write it again?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Every word. A friend's character is not to be adjusted to suit the opinion of the town.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: After Hume, who were your people?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: In Edinburgh, in my last years, Joseph Black the chemist and James Hutton the geologist. The three of us founded a club that met every week. We called it the Oyster Club, which sounds very grand and greedy, but no three men cared less for food. Hutton drank no wine, and Black lived on bread, a few prunes and milk and water. The conversation was free, never a lecture, and every interesting stranger who came to Edinburgh found his way to us.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And you? What was your vice?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Sugar. I confess it. Mr Walter Scott, who was a boy then, told the story of a tea party where I would not sit down, but walked round and round the table stealing lumps from the sugar basin, until the lady of the house put the basin on her own knee to protect it from me.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: The father of economics, banned from the sugar bowl.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: A clear case of a monopoly protecting itself against an inefficient consumer.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: You never married. Was there ever someone?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: You promised a love life, Mr Ram, and I fear you will be disappointed. When I was young there was a lady of great beauty and accomplishment. I was attached to her for several years. Nobody ever knew why nothing came of it, and I shall not tell you either. She never married, and neither did I.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: That's sad. And France?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: France was comic. At Abbeville there was a marquise, a woman of talent and wit, who had heard in Paris that I was Hume's great friend and nearly as great a philosopher. She resolved to make a conquest of me, and laid siege for days. I could not bear it, and I could not hide my embarrassment, which amused my companions extremely.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: You just weren't interested?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: My heart was otherwise engaged. There was an English lady staying at the same hotel. That is all I shall say, and more than I have said to anyone in two hundred years.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And your mother.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: She died in May 1784, in her ninetieth year. I had lived with her for sixty years. It was the first great sorrow of a life that had been, I must admit, singularly smooth. Some people said I grieved too much, as if I had no hope of seeing her again. I sat by her bed when the minister came, and joined in his prayers. Let them make of that what they like. I was never the same afterwards.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: I'm sorry.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Thank you. In my book on the moral sentiments I wrote that adversity depresses the mind much further below its natural state than prosperity can raise it above. I did not understand how true that was until she was gone.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Let's talk about money and success, because a lot of people watching this are young and ambitious. What does chasing wealth do to a person?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: I wrote a little portrait of such a person. "The poor man's son, whom Heaven in its anger has visited with ambition." He looks around and admires the condition of the rich. His father's cottage is too small. He would like to be carried about in a carriage. He imagines that if only he had all these things, he would sit still contentedly and be happy.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: That's literally every motivational video on the internet.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Then let me finish the story, since your videos apparently stop halfway. To get these things, in the very first year he submits to more fatigue and anxiety than he would have suffered his whole life without them. He works night and day. "He serves those whom he hates, and is obsequious to those whom he despises."

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: And at the end, in old age, his body worn with toil and disease, he discovers that "wealth and greatness are mere trinkets of frivolous utility." He has spent his life chasing an artificial repose, and for it he "sacrifices a real tranquillity that is at all times in his power."

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So you're saying don't be ambitious?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: No. I am saying be honest about what you are buying. The poor man's son also makes the world richer. Nature deceives us into thinking the trinkets will make us happy, and "It is this deception which rouses and keeps in continual motion the industry of mankind." It made us till the ground, build houses and found cities. It is good for the world. It is not always good for him.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Then what actually makes people happy?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: "What can be added to the happiness of the man who is in health, who is out of debt, and has a clear conscience?" Very little. Everything beyond that is decoration. And I said this was the natural and ordinary state of most men.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Health, no debt, clear conscience. That's it?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Between that condition and the highest pitch of prosperity, the difference is a trifle. Between that condition and real misery, the distance is immense. So guard your health, stay out of debt, and do nothing you would be ashamed to explain. Do that, and the rest is ornament.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: But you also wrote that the rich and poor aren't that different in happiness. That's hard to accept today, when the gap between rich and poor is enormous.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Push me on it. You should. I wrote that "the beggar, who suns himself by the side of the highway, possesses that security which kings are fighting for." I was speaking of peace of mind, not of comfort. But in The Wealth of Nations I said something harder: that the scanty maintenance of the labouring poor is the natural symptom that things are at a stand, and their starving condition that they are going fast backwards. A nation where working people are poorly paid is not a rich nation, however grand its palaces.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So no billionaire worship from you.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: I asked why we admire the rich so much. Not because we believe they are happier. "He does not even imagine that they are really happier than other people: but he imagines that they possess more means of happiness." We are dazzled by the machinery, not the result. Respect a man for what he does, not for the number of his contrivances.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Advice for a young person starting a career today?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Three things. First, find the work you can do better than your neighbours and give your whole attention to it. The tailor does not make his own shoes. And a mind fixed on one object is the mind that invents. Second, distrust any profession that pays you whether or not you do your duty. It will make you lazy, as it made the Oxford professors lazy. Third, keep a friend like David Hume, someone who will tell you the truth and tease you about it.

chapters.title: Hot takes: AI, influencers and India

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Hot takes round. I explain something quickly, you react. Ready?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: I have never been quick in my life, but I will try.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Artificial intelligence. Machines that can write, draw, answer questions, even do parts of a lawyer's or programmer's job. People are scared it will take their jobs.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Let me tell you about a boy. In the first steam engines, a boy was employed to open and close a valve as the piston rose and fell. One of these boys, who loved to play with his companions, tied a string from the handle of the valve to another part of the machine, so it worked by itself. One of the greatest improvements to that engine was "the discovery of a boy who wanted to save his own labour."

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So you're optimistic.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: I am optimistic about the engine. I would ask what became of the boy. Did he go back to play, or to some better work, or did he lose his place? I also warned that a man who spends his whole life on a few simple operations has no occasion to use his understanding, and becomes dull. If your thinking machines take the simple work and leave people the interesting work, wonderful. If they take the thinking and leave people only the pressing of buttons, then you must take care of their minds. In my day the remedy was a school in every parish.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Next. Social media influencers. People who post pictures of their lives for millions of strangers, and they get paid for attention.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: For attention alone? Not for any work?

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Often just attention.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Then I described them in 1759, without the pictures. There is a difference between the man who wants to be esteemed for what is really estimable and the man who wants praise on any terms. The first is easily satisfied. The second "is never to be satisfied, is full of jealousy and suspicion that we do not esteem him so much as he desires, because he has some secret consciousness that he desires more than he deserves."

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: You just roasted the entire internet.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: I roasted myself first. Every author wants praise. The question is whether he wants to be praiseworthy.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Is college worth it? University is incredibly expensive now. A lot of young people come out with huge debts.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Huge debts? Then my first question is whether the teachers work for the students' money or are paid regardless. I observed that the parts of education for which there are no public institutions are generally the best taught. A young man who goes to a fencing school "seldom fails of learning to fence." Because the fencing master is paid by his pupils, and if they do not learn, they do not come back.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Oxford, rich and endowed, taught me almost nothing. Glasgow, poor, where the professors depended in part on fees, gave me Hutcheson. So I would say: a university is worth exactly as much as it is made to care whether you learn. And if you must borrow to attend, borrow for the teacher, not the name.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Fake news, conspiracy theories. Misinformation spreads incredibly fast now.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: In my day we called it enthusiasm and superstition. I proposed two remedies. First, "Science is the great antidote to the poison of enthusiasm and superstition." Second, more surprisingly, public amusements: painting, poetry, music, dancing, plays. Gloomy, melancholy people are the easiest prey for fanatics. Theatre that laughs at fanatics does more than a hundred sermons.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So your answer to misinformation is science and comedy.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Science and comedy. Perhaps even a podcast.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Crypto. Digital money that no government issues. People buy it hoping it goes up, and some have become very rich and others have lost everything.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Money that no bank or king stands behind? Well, remember the nails of Fife. Money is whatever people will accept. So it is not impossible. But I lived through two lessons. The first was a Scotsman, John Law, who believed paper money could be multiplied to almost any extent. France adopted his scheme, and it became the Mississippi scheme, "the most extravagant project, both of banking and stock-jobbing, that perhaps the world ever saw." His "splendid but visionary ideas" still dazzled people in my day.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: The second I saw with my own eyes. In 1772 a great bank in Scotland, Douglas, Heron and Company, founded with the best intentions only three years before, collapsed and shook the whole country. Only three of thirty private banks in Edinburgh survived the crisis. My own pupil, the Duke, was one of its largest shareholders, and with liability unlimited nobody could say how much he would lose. I spent months helping my friends through it.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So your advice on crypto?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: The same as on any splendid new money. Ask who will pay you when you wish to be paid. If the answer is whoever buys it next, you are not holding money. You are holding hope.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Taxes. Everyone hates them. How should a government tax people?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: I gave four rules. People should pay in proportion to their abilities, that is, to the income they enjoy under the protection of the state. The tax should be certain, not arbitrary. It should be collected when it is convenient to pay. And it should take as little as possible beyond what reaches the treasury.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: The second rule is the one governments forget. When the tax is uncertain, everyone is at the mercy of the tax-gatherer. I wrote that "a very considerable degree of inequality, it appears, I believe, from the experience of all nations, is not near so great an evil as a very small degree of uncertainty."

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Says the man who became a tax collector.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: You are enjoying this too much, Mr Ram. We will come to that.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Last one, and it matters to a lot of our viewers. India. In your time, the British East India Company was taking over large parts of India. What did you think of it?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: I thought it was a disaster, and I said so. "The government of an exclusive company of merchants is, perhaps, the worst of all governments for any country whatever." A company that rules a country has the power to oppress the people and every temptation to do it.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: You wrote about Bengal specifically.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: I did. Bengal was a fertile country, where food should not have been hard to find, and yet "three or four hundred thousand people die of hunger in one year." When that happens in a fertile country, I wrote, you may be sure the funds that maintain the labouring poor are fast decaying. That was the state of Bengal under the Company. I set it beside North America, governed under the British constitution, and wrote that the difference between that and "the mercantile company which oppresses and domineers in the East Indies" could not be better illustrated than by the state of the two countries.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Today India is one of the largest and fastest-growing economies in the world. More than a billion people.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: A billion! Then here is my test, and it is the same for India as for Scotland. Do not ask how many palaces it has, or how much gold. Ask whether the wages of its working people are rising. "The liberal reward of labour, therefore, as it is the necessary effect, so it is the natural symptom of increasing national wealth." If that is happening for a billion people, it is the greatest thing I have heard today, and I include your telephone.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Let's talk about regrets. In your last years you had a government job. You were a Commissioner of Customs.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: You see the joke. The man who spent his best book attacking duties on trade spent his last twelve years collecting them. My father was a customs officer, and in the end so was I. I will say this: it taught me a great deal. I told a friend I would never have known or believed how essential practical knowledge was to understanding political subjects.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: There's a story about you and the doorman at the Customs House.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: I am told there is. I do not remember it, which my friends found the most remarkable part. Apparently the Board kept a porter in a great scarlet gown, with a staff seven feet high, who saluted each Commissioner at the door. He had saluted me perhaps five hundred times. One morning I saluted him back with my cane, followed him up the stairs, step for step, in exactly his posture, and bowed to him at the top with the utmost gravity.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: You marched behind him like a soldier.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: With complete seriousness, I am told. And when I came to myself I had no idea anything had happened. Usually, when my mind wandered at dinner, I could recover long stretches of the conversation afterwards. Not that time. I have no memory of it at all.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Here's the real regret question. Before you died, you had your friends burn your papers.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Sixteen volumes of manuscript. I was too weak to do it myself, so I begged Black and Hutton, two of my dearest friends, again and again. They kept putting me off, hoping I would recover or change my mind. A week before I died I sent for them and made them do it, there and then, without reading a page.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Why? Do you know what historians would give to read those?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: I know. But only a few of my papers were finished enough to deserve publication, and a man should be judged by the work he chose to finish, not by everything he scribbled. Still, I will be honest with you. I told a friend at the end that I regretted having done so little. I said I meant "to have done more, and there are materials in my papers of which I could have made a great deal." I had promised the world a book on law and government in 1759. I never wrote it.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: What did you spend your last year on?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Not on anything new. On my first book. The Theory of Moral Sentiments had been in the world thirty years and five editions, and I had never revised it. In my last year, though I was very ill, I went back to it and added a great deal. Of all the work I could have finished, I chose to finish that one.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: That says a lot about which book mattered to you.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Draw your own conclusions, Mr Ram. I have drawn mine.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So the father of economics died feeling unfinished.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Every honest man dies unfinished. Only fools die satisfied.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: How do you feel about how you're remembered? Politicians quote you. People put you on ties.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: On ties! Well. I would ask them to read both of my books, and all of the second. I said the consumer's interest was the end of all production. I said merchants conspire. I said wages should be liberal. I said the poor deserve education at public expense. If a man quotes the invisible hand and none of those, he has borrowed my hat and left the rest of me behind.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: We're at the end. One piece of advice for everyone watching.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Learn to see yourself as an impartial spectator would see you. Not as your mother sees you, nor your enemies, nor the crowd that applauds you. Ask what a fair-minded stranger would think, watching. Then live so that he would approve. It will not make you rich. It will make you someone worth knowing.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Now the show tradition. Every guest leaves a question for our next guest, without knowing who it will be. What's yours?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Let me think. Here it is. Was there something you left unfinished? And if your friends offered to save it from the fire, would you let them?

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: That's beautiful, and a bit dark.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: I am a Scotsman, sir. We do beautiful and a bit dark very well.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Last thing. What were your final words to your friends?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: It was a Sunday evening. My friends always came to supper on Sundays, and they came in good numbers that night. I went to bed early, and at the door I turned and said, "I love your company, gentlemen, but I believe I must leave you to go to another world." One of them remembers it a little differently: "I believe we must adjourn this meeting to some other place." Perhaps I said both.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Then let's adjourn this meeting. Adam Smith, thank you. This has been one of my favourite conversations.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Thank you, Mr Ram. You are a much better interviewer than the Oxford professors were teachers. That is faint praise, I know, but it is sincerely meant.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: That's our show. Remember, you've been listening to an AI recreation of Adam Smith, built from his books, his letters and John Rae's 1895 biography. Every source is in the description. If you want to meet the real Adam Smith, read The Theory of Moral Sentiments. I'm Ram. See you next time on The Deadman Show.

packaging.description:
Ram sits down with an AI recreation of Adam Smith, the Scottish philosopher who wrote The Wealth of Nations. They cover his kidnapping by gipsies at age three, being punished at Oxford for reading David Hume, starting the most famous economics book in history because he was bored in Toulouse, his friendship with Hume, a love he never explained, and why he had sixteen volumes of his own work burned a week before he died.

Smith also explains what people get wrong about the invisible hand, why chasing wealth can cost you your peace of mind, what he thought of the East India Company in Bengal, and how he'd judge AI, influencers and modern India. Adam Smith in this episode is an AI recreation built from his own writings and John Rae's public-domain biography (1895). His direct quotations come word for word from those sources.

essays-0024.title: Essays on Philosophical Subjects
essays-0024.location: The principles which lead and direct philosophical enquiries; as illustrated by the history of astronomy
essays-0024.text: Fire burns, and water refreshes; heavy bodies descend, and lighter substances fly upwards, by the necessity of their own nature; nor was the invisible hand of Jupiter ever apprehended to be employed in those matters. But thunder and lightning, storms and sunshine, those more irregular events, were ascribed to his favour, or his anger. Man, the only designing power with which they were acquainted, never acts but either to stop or to alter the course which natural events would take, if left to themselves. Those other intelligent beings, whom they imagined, but knew not, were naturally supposed to act in the same manner; not to employ themselves in supporting the ordinary course of things, which went on of its own accord, but to stop, to thwart, and to disturb it. And thus, in the first ages of the world, the lowest and most pusillanimous superstition supplied the place of philosophy. But when law has established order and security, and subsistence ceases to be precarious, the curiosity of mankind is increased, and their fears are diminished. The leisure which they then enjoy renders them more attentive to the appearances of nature, more observant of her smallest irregularities, and more desirous to know what is the chain which links them together. That some such chain subsists betwixt all her seemingly disjointed phenomena, they are necessarily led to conceive; and that magnanimity and cheerfulness which all generous natures acquire who are bred in civilized societies, where they have so few occasions to feel their weakness, and so many to be conscious of their strength and security, renders them less disposed to employ, for this connecting chain, those invisible beings whom the fear and ignorance of their rude forefathers had engendered. Those of liberal fortunes, whose attention is not much occupied either with business or with pleasure, can fill up the void of their imagination, which is thus disengaged from the ordinary affairs of life, no other way than by attending to that train of events which passes around them. While the great objects of nature thus pass in review before them, many things occur in an order to which they have not been accustomed. Their imagination, which accompanies with ease and delight the regular progress of nature, is stopped and embarrassed by those seeming incoherences; they excite their wonder, and seem to require some chain of intermediate events, which, by connecting them with something that has gone before, may thus render the whole course of the universe consistent and of a piece. Wonder, therefore, and not any expectation of advantage from its discoveries, is the first principle which prompts mankind to the study of Philosophy, of that science which pretends to lay open the concealed connections that unite the various appearances of nature; and they pursue this study for its own sake, as an original pleasure or good in itself, without regarding its tendency to procure them the means of many other pleasures.

rae-0002.title: Life of Adam Smith, by John Rae
rae-0002.location: Chapter I. Early days at kirkcaldy 1723-1737
rae-0002.text: Smith's father died in the spring of 1723, a few months before his famous son was born. Some doubt has been cast upon this fact by an announcement quoted by President M'Cosh, in his Scottish Philosophy, from the Scots Magazine of 1740, of the promotion of Adam Smith, Comptroller of the Customs, Kirkcaldy, to be Inspector-General of the Outports. But conclusive evidence exists of the date of the death of Smith's father in a receipt for his funeral expenses, which is in the possession of Professor Cunningham, and which, as a curious illustration of the habits of the time, I subjoin in a note below. The promotion of 1740 is the promotion not of Smith's father but of his cousin, whom I have just had occasion to mention, and who appears from Chamberlayne's Notitia Angliæ to have been Comptroller of the Customs at Kirkcaldy from about 1734 till somewhere before 1741. In the Notitia Angliæ for 1741 the name of Adam Smith ceases to appear as Comptroller in Kirkcaldy, and appears for the first time as Inspector-General of the Outports, exactly in accordance with the intimation quoted by Dr. M'Cosh. It is curious that Smith, who was to do so much to sweep away the whole system of the Customs, should have been so closely connected with that branch of administration. His father, his only known relation on his father's side, and himself, were all officials in the Scotch Customs.

rae-0003.title: Life of Adam Smith, by John Rae
rae-0003.location: Chapter I. Early days at kirkcaldy 1723-1737
rae-0003.text: On the mother's side his kindred were much connected with the army. His uncle, Robert Douglas of Strathendry, and three of his uncle's sons were military officers, and so was his cousin, Captain Skene, the laird of the neighbouring estate of Pitlour. Colonel Patrick Ross, a distinguished officer of the times, was also a relation, but on which side I do not know. His mother herself was from first to last the heart of Smith's life. He being an only child, and she an only parent, they had been all in all to one another during his infancy and boyhood, and after he was full of years and honours her presence was the same shelter to him as it was when a boy. His friends often spoke of the beautiful affection and worship with which he cherished her. One who knew him well for the last thirty years of his life, and was very probably at one time a boarder in his house, the clever and bustling Earl of Buchan, elder brother of Lord Chancellor Erskine, says the principal avenue to Smith's heart always was by his mother. He was a delicate child, and afflicted even in childhood with those fits of absence and that habit of speaking to himself which he carried all through life. Of his infancy only one incident has come down to us. In his fourth year, while on a visit to his grandfather's house at Strathendry on the banks of the Leven, the child was stolen by a passing band of gipsies, and for a time could not be found. But presently a gentleman arrived who had met a gipsy woman a few miles down the road carrying a child that was crying piteously. Scouts were immediately despatched in the direction indicated, and they came upon the woman in Leslie wood. As soon as she saw them she threw her burden down and escaped, and the child was brought back to his mother. He would have made, I fear, a poor gipsy. As he grew up in boyhood his health became stronger, and he was in due time sent to the Burgh School of Kirkcaldy.

rae-0004.title: Life of Adam Smith, by John Rae
rae-0004.location: Chapter I. Early days at kirkcaldy 1723-1737
rae-0004.text: The Burgh School of Kirkcaldy was one of the best secondary schools of Scotland at that period, and its principal master, Mr. David Millar, had the name of being one of the best schoolmasters of his day. When Smith first went to school we cannot say, but it seems probable that he began Latin in 1733, for Eutropius is the class-book of a beginner in Latin, and the Eutropius which Smith used as a class-book still exists, and contains his signature with the date of that year. As he left school in 1737, he thus had at least four years' training in the classics before he proceeded to the University. Millar, his classical master, had adventured in literature. He wrote a play, and his pupils used to act it. Acting plays was in those days a common exercise in the higher schools of Scotland. The presbyteries often frowned, and tried their best to stop the practice, but the town councils, which had the management of these schools, resented the dictation of the presbyteries, and gave the drama not only the support of their personal presence at the performances, but sometimes built a special stage and auditorium for the purpose. Sir James Steuart, the economist, played the king in Henry the Fourth when he was a boy at the school of North Berwick in 1735.

rae-0007.title: Life of Adam Smith, by John Rae
rae-0007.location: Chapter I. Early days at kirkcaldy 1723-1737
rae-0007.text: A small town like Kirkcaldy--it had then only 1500 inhabitants--is a not unfavourable observatory for beginning one's knowledge of the world. It has more sorts and conditions of men to exhibit than a rural district can furnish, and it exhibits each more completely in all their ways, pursuits, troubles, characters, than can possibly be done in a city. Smith, who, spite of his absence of mind, was always an excellent observer, would grow up in the knowledge of all about everybody in that little place, from the "Lady Dunnikier," the great lady of the town, to its poor colliers and salters who were still bondsmen. Kirkcaldy, too, had its shippers trading with the Baltic, its customs officers, with many a good smuggling story, and it had a nailery or two, which Smith is said to have been fond of visiting as a boy, and to have acquired in them his first rough idea of the value of division of labour. However that may be, Smith does draw some of his illustrations of the division of labour from that particular business, which would necessarily be very familiar to his mind, and it may have been in Kirkcaldy that he found the nailers paid their wages in nails, and using these nails afterwards as a currency in making their purchases from the shopkeepers.

rae-0008.title: Life of Adam Smith, by John Rae
rae-0008.location: Chapter I. Early days at kirkcaldy 1723-1737
rae-0008.text: At school Smith was marked for his studious disposition, his love of reading, and his power of memory; and by the age of fourteen he had advanced sufficiently in classics and mathematics to be sent to Glasgow College, with a view to obtaining a Snell exhibition to Oxford.

rae-0009.title: Life of Adam Smith, by John Rae
rae-0009.location: Chapter II. Student at glasgow college a.d. 1737-1740. aet. 14-17
rae-0009.text: Smith entered Glasgow College in 1737, no doubt in October, when the session began, and he remained there till the spring of 1740. The arts curriculum at that time extended over five sessions, so that Smith did not complete the course required for a degree. In the three sessions he attended he would go through the classes of Latin, Greek, Mathematics, and Moral Philosophy, and have thus listened to the lectures of the three eminent teachers who were then drawing students to this little western College from the most distant quarters, and keeping its courts alive with a remarkable intellectual activity. Dr. A. Carlyle, who came to Glasgow College for his divinity classes after he had finished his arts course at Edinburgh, says he found a spirit of inquiry and a zeal for learning abroad among the students of Glasgow which he remembered nothing like among the students of Edinburgh. This intellectual awakening was the result mainly of the teaching of three professors--Alexander Dunlop, Professor of Greek, a man of fine scholarship and taste, and an unusually engaging method of instruction; Robert Simson, the professor of Mathematics, an original if eccentric genius, who enjoyed a European reputation as the restorer of the geometry of the ancients; and above all, Francis Hutcheson, a thinker of great original power, and an unrivalled academic lecturer.

rae-0012.title: Life of Adam Smith, by John Rae
rae-0012.location: Chapter II. Student at glasgow college a.d. 1737-1740. aet. 14-17
rae-0012.text: Matthew Stewart of Edinburgh, never seemed to feel even the slightest uneasiness from the neglect with which the ignorance of the public received some of their most valuable works." And it ought to be remembered that when Smith wrote thus of Simson he had been long intimate with D'Alembert. But while Smith improved his Greek under Dunlop, and acquired a distinct ardour for mathematics under the inspiring instructions of Simson, the most powerful and enduring influence he came under at Glasgow was undoubtedly that of Hutcheson--"the never-to-be-forgotten Hutcheson," as he styled him half a century later in recalling his obligations to his old College on the occasion of his election to the Rectorship. No other man, indeed, whether teacher or writer, did so much to awaken Smith's mind or give a bent to his ideas. He is sometimes considered a disciple of Hume and sometimes considered a disciple of Quesnay; if he was any man's disciple, he was Hutcheson's. Hutcheson was exactly the stamp of man fitted to stir and mould the thought of the young. He was, in the first place, one of the most impressive lecturers that ever spoke from an academic chair. Dugald Stewart, who knew many of his pupils, states that every one of them told of the extraordinary impression his lectures used to make on their hearers. He was the first professor in Glasgow to give up lecturing in Latin and speak to his audience in their own tongue, and he spoke without notes and with the greatest freedom and animation. Nor was it only his eloquence, but his ideas themselves were rousing. Whatever he touched upon, he treated, as we may still perceive from his writings, with a certain freshness and decided originality which must have provoked the dullest to some reflection, and in a bracing spirit of intellectual liberty which it was strength and life for the young mind to breathe.

rae-0017.title: Life of Adam Smith, by John Rae
rae-0017.location: Chapter II. Student at glasgow college a.d. 1737-1740. aet. 14-17
rae-0017.text: These Snell exhibitions, which were practically in the gift of the Glasgow professors, were naturally the prize of the best student of Glasgow College at the time they fell vacant, and they have been held in the course of the two centuries of their existence by many distinguished men, including Sir William Hamilton and Lockhart, Archbishop Tait and Lord President Inglis. They were originally founded by an old Glasgow student, a strong Episcopalian, for the purpose of educating Scotchmen for the service of the Episcopal Church in Scotland. By the terms of his will the holders were even to be bound under penalty of £500 "to enter holy orders and return to serve the Church in Scotland," and it has sometimes been concluded from that circumstance that Smith must have accepted the Snell exhibition with a view to the Episcopal ministry. But the original purpose of the founder was frustrated by the Revolution settlement, which made "the Church in Scotland" Presbyterian, and left scarce any Episcopal remnant to serve, and the original condition has never been practically enforced. The last attempt to impose it was made during Smith's own tenure of the exhibition, and failed. In the year 1744 the Vice-Chancellor and the heads of Colleges at Oxford raised a process in the Court of Chancery for compelling the Snell exhibitioners "to submit and conform to the doctrines and discipline of the Church of England, and to enter into holy orders when capable thereof by the canons of the Church of England"; but the Court of Chancery refused to interfere, and the exhibitioners were left entirely free to choose their sect, their profession, and their country, as seemed best to themselves. It may be added that in Smith's time the Snell foundation yielded five exhibitions of £40 a year each, tenable for eleven years.

rae-0025.title: Life of Adam Smith, by John Rae
rae-0025.text: There was only one fruit in the garden of which he might not freely eat, and that was the productions of modern rationalism. A story has come down which, though not mentioned by Dugald Stewart, is stated by M'Culloch to rest on the best authority, and by Dr. Strang of Glasgow to have been often told by Smith himself, to the effect that he was one day detected reading Hume's Treatise of Human Nature--probably the very copy presented him by the author at the apparent suggestion of Hutcheson--and was punished by a severe reprimand and the confiscation of the evil book. It is at least entirely consistent with all we know of the spirit of darkness then ruling in Oxford that it should be considered an offence of peculiar aggravation for a student to read a great work of modern thought which had been actually placed in his hands by his professor at Glasgow, and the only wonder is that Smith escaped so lightly, for but a few years before three students were expelled from Oxford for coquetting with Deism, and a fourth, of whom better hopes seem to have been formed, had his degree deferred for two years, and was required in the interval to translate into Latin as a reformatory exercise the whole of Leslie's Short and Easy Method with the Deists.

rae-0027.title: Life of Adam Smith, by John Rae
rae-0027.text: But low health was only one of the miseries of his estate at Oxford. There is reason to believe that Balliol College was in his day a stepmother to her Scotch sons, and that their existence there was made very uncomfortable not merely at the hands of the mob of young gentlemen among whom they were obliged to live, but even more by the unfair and discriminating harshness of the College authorities themselves. Out of the hundred students then residing at Balliol, eight at least were Scotch, four on the Snell foundation and four on the Warner, and the Scotch eight seem to have been always treated as an alien and intrusive faction. The Snell exhibitioners were continually complaining to the Glasgow Senatus on the subject, and the Glasgow Senatus thought them perfectly justified in complaining. In a letter of 22nd May 1776, in which they go over the whole long story of grievances, the Glasgow Senatus tell the Master and Fellows of Balliol plainly that the Scotch students had never been "welcomely received" at Balliol, and had never been happy there. If an English undergraduate committed a fault, the authorities never thought of blaming any one but himself, but when one of the eight Scotch undergraduates did so, his sin was remembered against all the other seven, and reflections were cast on the whole body; "a circumstance," add the Senatus, "which has been much felt during their residence at Balliol." Their common resentment against the injustice of this kind of tribal accountability that was imposed on them naturally provoked a common resistance; it developed "a spirit of association," say the Senatus, which "has at all periods been a cause of much trouble both to Balliol and to Glasgow Colleges." In 1744, when Smith himself was one of them, the Snell exhibitioners wrote an account of their grievances to the Glasgow Senatus, and stated "what they wanted to be done towards making their residence more easy and advantageous"; and in 1753, when some of Smith's contemporaries would still be on the foundation, Dr. Leigh, the master of Balliol, tells the Glasgow Senatus that he had ascertained in an interview with one of the Snell exhibitioners that what they wanted was to be transferred to some other college, because they had "a total dislike to Balliol."

rae-0044.title: Life of Adam Smith, by John Rae
rae-0044.location: Chapter V. Professor at glasgow 1751-1764. aet. 27-40
rae-0044.text: The Edinburgh lectures soon bore fruit. On the death of Mr. Loudon, Professor of Logic in Glasgow College, in 1750, Smith was appointed to the vacant chair, and so began that period of thirteen years of active academic work which he always looked back upon, he tells us, "as by far the most useful and therefore by far the happiest and most honourable period" of his life. The appointment lay with the Senatus--or, more strictly, with a section of the Senatus known as the Faculty Professors--some of whom, of course, had been his own teachers ten years before, and knew him well; and the minutes state that the choice was unanimous. He was elected on the 9th of January 1751, and was admitted to the office on the 16th, after reading a dissertation De origine idearum, signing the Westminster Confession of Faith before the Presbytery of Glasgow, and taking the usual oath De fideli to the University authorities; but he did not begin work till the opening of the next session in October. His engagements in Edinburgh did not permit of his undertaking his duties in Glasgow earlier, and his classes were accordingly conducted, with the sanction of the Senatus, by Dr. Hercules Lindsay, the Professor of Jurisprudence, as his substitute, from the beginning of January till the end of June.

rae-0054.title: Life of Adam Smith, by John Rae
rae-0054.text: In Smith's day there were only some 300 students at Glasgow College in all, and the Moral Philosophy chair alone had never more than 80 or 90 in the public class and 20 in the private. The public class did not mean a free class, as it does on the Continent; it really was the dearer of the two, the fee in the private class being only a guinea, while the fee of the public class was a guinea and a half. The public class was the ordinary class taken for graduation and other purposes, and obligatory by academic authority; the private was a special class, undertaken, with the permission of the Senatus, for those who wished to push the subject further; and to harmonise this account of them with what has been previously said of the income Smith drew from fees, it is necessary to explain that many of the students who attended these classes paid no fees, according to a custom which still prevails in Scotch universities, and by which one was considered a civis of a class he had attended for two years, and might thereafter attend it whenever he chose without charge. Many in this way attended the Moral Philosophy class four or five years, and among them, as Dr. Reid informs us, quite a number of preachers and advanced students of divinity and law, before whom, the worthy doctor confesses, he used to stand in awe to speak without the most careful preparation.

rae-0058.title: Life of Adam Smith, by John Rae
rae-0058.text: Millar, it may be added, was one of Smith's favourite pupils, and after obtaining the chair of Jurisprudence in his old College, one of his chief associates, and Smith held so high an opinion of Millar's unique powers as a stimulating teacher that he sent his cousin, David Douglas, to Glasgow College for no other purpose but to have the advantage of the lectures and conversation of Millar. Jeffrey used to say that the most bracing exercises a student in Glasgow underwent in those days were the supper disputations at Professor Millar's house, and that, able and learned as his works are, "they revealed nothing of that magical vivacity which made his conversation and his lectures still more full of delight than of instruction." Though he always refused to accept Smith's doctrine of free trade, Millar was the most effective and influential apostle of Liberalism in Scotland in that age, and Jeffrey's father could never forgive himself for having put his son to Glasgow, where, though he was strictly forbidden to enter Millar's class-room, "the mere vicinity of Millar's influence" had sent him back a Liberal. Now it is this interesting and famous lecturer from whom we obtain the fullest account of Smith's qualities as a lecturer and of the substance of his lectures. "In the professorship of logic," he says, "to which Mr. Smith was appointed on his first introduction into this University, he soon saw the necessity of departing widely from the plan that had been followed by his predecessors, and of directing the attention of his pupils to studies of a more interesting and useful nature than the logic and metaphysics of the schools. Accordingly, after exhibiting a general view of the powers of the mind, and explaining as much of the ancient logic as was requisite to gratify curiosity with respect to an artificial method of reasoning which had once occupied the universal attention of the learned, he dedicated all the rest of his time to the delivering of a system of rhetoric and belles-lettres."

rae-0152.title: Life of Adam Smith, by John Rae
rae-0152.location: Chapter IX. The "theory of moral sentiments" 1759. aet. 36
rae-0152.text: Non, si quid turbida Roma Elevet, accedas: examenve improbum in iliâ Castiges trutinâ: nec te quaesiveris extra. A wise man's kingdom is his own heart; or, if he ever looks farther, it will only be to the judgment of a select few, who are free from prejudices and capable of examining; his work. Nothing, indeed, can be a stronger presumption of falsehood than the approbation of the multitude; and Phocion, you know, always suspected himself of some blunder when he was attended with the applause of the populace. Supposing, therefore, that you have duly prepared yourself for the worst by all these reflections, I proceed to tell you the melancholy news that your book has been very unfortunate, for the public seem disposed to applaud it extremely. It was looked for by the foolish people with some impatience; and the mob of literati are beginning already to be very loud in its praises. Three bishops called yesterday at Millar's shop in order to buy copies, and to ask questions about the author. The Bishop of Peterborough said he had passed the evening in a company where he heard it extolled above all books in the world. The Duke of Argyle is more decisive than he used to be in its favour. I suppose he either considers it as an exotic, or thinks the author will be very serviceable to him in the Glasgow elections. Lord Lyttelton says that Robertson and Smith and Bower are the glories of English literature. Oswald protests he does not know whether he has reaped more instruction or entertainment from it, but you may easily judge what reliance can be placed on his judgment. He has been engaged all his life in public business, and he never sees any faults in his friends. Millar exults and brags that two-thirds of the edition are already sold, and that he is now sure of success. You see what a son of the earth that is, to value books only by the profit they bring him. In that view, I believe, it may prove a very good book.

rae-0153.title: Life of Adam Smith, by John Rae
rae-0153.location: Chapter IX. The "theory of moral sentiments" 1759. aet. 36
rae-0153.text: Charles Townshend, who passes for the cleverest fellow in England, is so much taken with the performance that he said to Oswald he would put the Duke of Buccleugh under the author's care, and would make it worth his while to accept of that charge. As soon as I heard this I called on him twice with a view of talking with him about the matter, and of convincing him of the propriety of sending that young gentleman to Glasgow, for I could not hope that he could offer you any terms which would tempt you to renounce your professorship; but I missed him. Mr. Townshend passes for being a little uncertain in his resolutions, so perhaps you need not build much on his sally. In recompense for so many mortifying things, which nothing but truth could have extorted from me, and which I could easily have multiplied to a greater number, I doubt not but you are so good a Christian as to return good for evil, and to flatter my vanity by telling me that all the godly in Scotland abuse me for my account of John Knox and the Reformation. I suppose you are glad to see my paper end, and that I am obliged to conclude with--Your humble servant. On the 28th of July Hume again writes from London on the same subject:--

rae-0180.title: Life of Adam Smith, by John Rae
rae-0180.location: Chapter XI > C. townshend. lady dalkeith presents her compliments to you. adderbury, 25th october 1763
rae-0180.text: Smith accepted the offer. The terms were a salary of £300 a year, with travelling expenses while abroad, and a pension of £300 a year for life afterwards. He was thus to have twice his Glasgow income, and to have it assured till death. The pension was no doubt a principal inducement to a Scotch professor in those days to take such a post, for a Scotch professor had then no resource in his old age except the price he happened to receive for his chair from his successor in the event of his resignation; and we find several of them--Professors Moor and Robert Simson of Glasgow among others--much harassed with pecuniary cares in their last years. Smith's remuneration was liberal, but nothing beyond what was usual in such situations at the time. Dr. John Moore, who gave up his medical practice in Glasgow a few years later to be tutor to the young Duke of Hamilton, got also £300 a year while actively employed in the tutorship and a pension of £100 a year afterwards. Professor Rouet, who, as already mentioned, sacrificed his chair in Glasgow for his tutorial appointment, is said to have received a pension of £500 a year from Lord Hopetoun, in addition to a pension of £50 he received, in consideration of previous services of the same kind, from Sir John Maxwell; and Professor Adam Ferguson, who was appointed tutor to the Earl of Chesterfield on Smith's recommendation, had £400 a year while on duty, and a pension of £200 a year, which he lived to enjoy for forty years after, receiving from first to last nearly £9000 for his two years' work. Smith did almost as well, for with the pension, which he drew for twenty-four years, he got altogether more than £8000 for his three years' service.

rae-0185.title: Life of Adam Smith, by John Rae
rae-0185.text: His parting with his students was not quite so simple. They made some difficulty, as he seems to have anticipated, about taking back the fees they had paid him for his class, and he was obliged to resort almost to force before he succeeded in getting them to do so. The curious scene is described by Alexander Fraser Tytler (Lord Woodhouselee) in his Life of Lord Kames: "After concluding his last lecture, and publicly announcing from the chair that he was now taking a final leave of his auditors, acquainting them at the same time with the arrangements he had made, to the best of his power, for their benefit, he drew from his pocket the several fees of the students, wrapped up in separate paper parcels, and beginning to call up each man by his name, he delivered to the first who was called the money into his hand. The young man peremptorily refused to accept it, declaring that the instruction and pleasure he had already received was much more than he either had repaid or ever could compensate, and a general cry was heard from every one in the room to the same effect. But Mr. Smith was not to be bent from his purpose. After warmly expressing his feelings of gratitude and the strong sense he had of the regard shown to him by his young friends, he told them this was a matter betwixt him and his own mind, and that he could not rest satisfied unless he performed what he deemed right and proper. 'You must not refuse me this satisfaction; nay, by heavens, gentlemen, you shall not;' and seizing by the coat the young man who stood next him, he thrust the money into his pocket and then pushed him from him. The rest saw it was in vain to contest the matter, and were obliged to let him have his own way."

rae-0186.title: Life of Adam Smith, by John Rae
